questions.q: Teena orders a lamp listed at Rs 900 on a shopping app. The seller is in another city, she pays online and the lamp is delivered. Her classmate says, 'This is not a market, because Teena never met the seller.' Which reply is correct?
o: It is a market: both sides agreed a price, and markets can be online
It is not a market: a market must have a building where goods are kept
It is a market only because the goods were delivered to her doorstep
It is not a market: only a bazaar or haat can be called a market place
questions.a: The chapter says a market can be at a physical place or online, and every market has a buyer, a seller and an agreed price. The lamp sale has all three. Delivery is not what makes it a market, and a building is not required.

questions.q: A family spends Rs 9,000 in a month: Rs 3,500 on food, Rs 1,500 on clothes for the children, Rs 2,000 on rent for their home, Rs 500 on a streaming subscription and Rs 1,500 on upgrading to a newer phone. Taking food, clothing and shelter as needs, as the chapter does, the money spent on wants is Rs ___.
Anil says, 'Whatever I spend on every single day is a need.' Which item from his daily spending shows that he is wrong, going by the chapter's definition of a need?
o: Rs 40 on a cold drink each evening, which he buys daily but could do without
Rs 15 on drinking water each day
Rs 10 on a packet of milk for the family's morning tea each day
Rs 60 on the lunch that he eats at school each day
questions.a: A need is something a person requires to survive, such as food, water, clothing and shelter. The cold drink is bought daily but is desired and not essential, so it is a want; buying something often does not make it a need. Drinking water, milk and lunch (food) are needs.

questions.q:
A guava seller asks Rs 80 per kg. A buyer offers Rs 30. After some bargaining they settle at Rs 45 per kg and the buyer takes 2 kg.
1. Rs 45 per kg is the price in this transaction, because it is the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller is willing to sell.
2. Rs 80 per kg is the price, because the seller named it first and the buyer must accept it.
3. If the two had not reached an amount both accepted, the transaction might not have taken place.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 follow the chapter: price is the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller willing to sell, and without such a point the transaction may not take place. Statement 2 is false: a seller's first ask is not the price; buyer and seller negotiate until a mutually agreeable price is reached.

questions.q:
The history club of a Bengaluru school puts up this extract at its exhibition. Fernao Nuniz wrote: 'There were craftsmen, also, working in their streets, so that you saw made there golden jewels and gewgaws... sellers of cloths... it is a mystery how there should be an abundance of everything therein.' Domingos Paes listed grains, seeds, milk, oil, silk, cows, horses, quails and partridges.
(a) Sort these four goods into needs and wants, using the chapter's definitions: grains, milk, golden jewels, rubies.
(b) Many foreign accounts, like these two, described the bazaar. Which statement in the chapter about what markets do does the fame of the bazaar in other lands best illustrate?
(c) The extract speaks of sellers and goods but never mentions a price. Which feature of a market is therefore not visible in it, and why must it have existed for any sale in the bazaar to happen?
(d) The club must choose one caption for the entrance: (i) 'Hampi: where every kind of good, from grain to rubies, could be had in one place' or (ii) 'Hampi: where craftsmen made in their streets what they sold'. Choose one and justify it using the extract.
questions.a: (a) Grains and milk are needs (required to survive); golden jewels and rubies are wants (desired but not essential for survival). (b) Markets connect people, traditions and ideas, beyond supplying goods. (c) The price: a buyer and a seller must agree on a price at which the transaction takes place, so a sale cannot have happened without one even though the extract does not name it. (d) Either caption is defensible if justified: (i) rests on Paes's long list and the 'abundance of everything'; (ii) rests on Nuniz's craftsmen working in the streets where jewels and cloth were on sale. Marks go for a choice tied to words of the extract.
s: Part (a): grains and milk as needs, jewels and rubies as wants, with the definitions
Part (b): markets connect people, traditions and ideas
Part (c): price named as the missing feature and why a sale needs an agreed price
Part (d): a caption chosen and justified from the extract

questions.q: True or False? 'Because Fernao Nuniz called Hampi a barren country, the chapter shows that the Hampi Bazaar had very few goods on sale.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Nuniz wrote that the country was barren and yet found it a mystery how there should be an abundance of everything in it. The bazaar had grains, oil, silk, animals, jewels and cloth in great quantity, so 'barren' described the land, not the market.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: Nuniz marvelled at the abundance in a barren land, so the bazaar was well stocked

questions.q: At a school fair, Dhruv wants a pen-holder and Alia has made one, and both are keen. They walk away from each other without a sale because they cannot settle on the money to be paid. Which feature of a market is missing?
questions.a: Every market has a buyer and a seller, and both must agree on a price for the transaction to take place. Here the buyer and seller exist, so what is missing is an agreed price.
o: A price both sides accept
A buyer who is interested in the product
A seller who has the product to offer
A shop building to hold the goods

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A place can be called a market only if buyers and sellers meet there in person.
Reason (R): Goods and services become available to individuals, households and businesses through markets.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: R is a statement from the chapter, so it is true. A is false: the chapter says a market can be at a physical place or online, and buyers and sellers can transact from thousands of kilometres apart. R does not support the 'only in person' idea.

questions.q: A family's shopping list has rice, a school-uniform shirt, a gaming headset and a can of drinking water. (a) Which items are needs by the chapter's definition? (b) Which item is a want, and what makes it one?
questions.a: (a) Rice, the uniform shirt (clothing) and drinking water. (b) The gaming headset: it is something a person desires but is not essential for survival.
s: Part (a): rice, shirt (clothing) and water identified as needs
Part (b): headset named as the want, because it is desired but not essential for survival

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the chapter term in Column B that describes it.
Column A: 1. Rs 50, the amount Aman and Bina both accept for a bookmark  2. A family buys a second television for its larger screen  3. A family buys drinking water for the day  4. An order placed on a phone from another city is delivered to the door
Column B: a. a want  b. price  c. a need  d. an online market
questions.a: Rs 50, the accepted amount, is the price; the larger-screen television is desired and not essential, so a want; drinking water is required to survive, so a need; an order on a phone delivered to the door is an online market. The wrong pairings swap need and want or confuse price with the market.

questions.q: Imran says, 'A market is only about money. Nothing else happens there.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. 'Only' is too strong. The chapter says markets supply goods and services that people need and want, and in addition markets connect people, traditions and ideas. So markets do more than move money.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'only'
States that markets supply goods and services people need and want
States that markets also connect people, traditions and ideas

questions.q: Mohan runs a mathematics class online and charges Rs 400 a month per student. Seema's father pays by phone each month. (a) Name the buyer, the seller and the price in this arrangement and say whether it is a market. (b) Is Mohan selling a good or a service, and does the chapter allow it to be traded online?
questions.a: (a) Buyer: Seema's father (on behalf of Seema); seller: Mohan; price: Rs 400 a month. It is a market, since it has a buyer, a seller and an agreed price, and a market can be online. (b) A service. The chapter names online classes as a service one can use without leaving home, with payment made online.
s: Part (a): buyer, seller, price named and judged a market
Part (b): service, and online classes allowed by the chapter

questions.q:
A class runs a one-day stall. In the first hour 30 buyers purchase bottles of drinking water at Rs 10 each, but only 6 buy friendship bands at the asked price of Rs 60. The stall then lowers the band price to Rs 40 and 14 buy in the next hour.
(a) Classify water and bands as need or want.
(b) Work out the money taken from bands in each hour.
(c) What does the change in sales show about the price in a market, and what may have happened if the stall had refused to move below Rs 60?
(d) Name one thing these figures do not tell the class before it can say whether lowering the price was wise.
questions.a: (a) Water is a need (required to survive); bands are a want (desired, not essential). (b) 6 x 60 = Rs 360 in the first hour; 14 x 40 = Rs 560 in the next. (c) Price is the amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell. Buyers found Rs 60 too high; at Rs 40 more were willing. If the stall had held at Rs 60, no price acceptable to both might have been reached and the sales might not have taken place. (d) The cost of making the bands, because the chapter says a seller will not sell at a price that is not profitable; more money taken does not show profit.
s: Part (a): water as need, bands as want
Part (b): Rs 360 and Rs 560
Part (c): price as the amount both accept, with the effect of holding at Rs 60
Part (d): cost or profit named as the missing information

questions.q: At a village fair, farmers from three villages explain their seed-saving methods to buyers while selling vegetables, and buyers from two communities share recipes with them. Which role of markets, named in the chapter, does this show best, in addition to supplying goods?
o: Markets connect people, traditions and ideas
Markets fix the price of goods before any buyer arrives
Markets can be only at a physical place
Markets deal only in goods and never in services
questions.a: The chapter says that markets, besides supplying goods and services, connect people, traditions and ideas. The fair shows people from different places exchanging ideas while trading. The other options are either not stated by the chapter or contradict it.

questions.q: At a fair, Aman hands over Rs 50 and receives a handmade bookmark from Bina after the two have agreed on that amount. (a) Which part of the event is the trade and which is the price? (b) Why is price not the same thing as trade?
questions.a: (a) The exchange of the bookmark for the money is the trade (buying and selling); Rs 50 is the price. (b) Price is only the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller willing to sell; trade is the whole buying, selling or exchange of goods and services, which is completed once that price is agreed.
s: Part (a): exchange of bookmark for money as trade, Rs 50 as price
Part (b): price is the agreed amount, trade is the whole exchange it completes

questions.q: Describe a purchase at your school's annual-day fair in three or four sentences so that it shows a buyer, a seller and a price. Mark each of the three in your account.
questions.a: Any suitable account, e.g. 'Meera (buyer) asks Tarun (seller) for a bookmark. He asks Rs 20; she offers Rs 15; they settle at Rs 18, and she pays.' It must name a buyer, a seller and an agreed price.
s: A buyer clearly shown
A seller clearly shown
A price on which both agree, so the transaction is completed

questions.q:
Imtiaz sells dry fruits at a Sunday haat. About 40 customers come each week and the average bill is Rs 200; the dry fruit in that bill costs him Rs 140. A friend suggests he also sell on a shopping app. He expects 25 app orders a week from other cities at Rs 260 each. For each app order the goods cost him Rs 180, the app takes a commission of Rs 40 and packing and posting cost Rs 35. Packing takes him 8 extra hours a week.
(a) Which two features from the chapter make an app sale a market even though the buyer never visits his stall?
(b) An app buyer offers Rs 250 instead of Rs 260. Using the chapter's idea of the seller's side of price, should he accept? Work out his gain or loss per order at Rs 250.
(c) Work out his weekly profit from the haat and from the app at Rs 260.
(d) Decide whether he should add the app, using the figures and one point from the chapter other than money.
questions.a: (a) A buyer and a seller who agree on a price; the chapter says a market can be physical or online. (b) Cost per order = 180 + 40 + 35 = Rs 255, so at Rs 250 he loses Rs 5 per order. The chapter says a seller may not sell at a price that is not profitable, so he should refuse. (c) Haat: 40 x (200 - 140) = Rs 2,400. App: 25 x (260 - 255) = Rs 125. (d) Either choice can be defended. Add: the app earns an extra Rs 125 and reaches buyers in other cities who could never visit a haat. Do not add: Rs 125 for 8 hours is small and any rise in commission turns it into a loss. The answer must use Rs 125 and a non-money point such as reach or effort.
s: Part (a): buyer, seller and agreed price; online allowed
Part (b): Rs 255 cost, loss of Rs 5, seller will not sell unprofitably
Part (c): Rs 2,400 at the haat and Rs 125 on the app
Part (d): a decision using Rs 125 and a non-money point

questions.q: Rekha buys a book on a shopping app at the printed price of Rs 350 and says, 'I could not bargain, so no price was agreed and this was not a market.' (a) Is her conclusion right? (b) In what way did she and the seller still agree on a price?
questions.a: (a) No. A market needs a buyer, a seller and a price, and it can be online. (b) The seller offered the book at Rs 350 and Rekha was willing to buy at that amount and paid it. Price is the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller willing to sell, so her payment is her agreement even without bargaining.
s: Part (a): conclusion rejected, online market allowed
Part (b): the printed price was accepted by her paying it

questions.q: Compare the Hampi Bazaar of the 16th century with an online shopping app of today. State what is common to both and what is different, and then say what this tells you about the features of any market.
questions.a: Common: each has buyers and sellers, goods, and a price to be agreed, and each connects people. Different: Hampi was a physical place where buyers met sellers face to face, while an app lets them transact from thousands of kilometres apart with goods delivered to the doorstep and payment online. So the essential features are a buyer, a seller and an agreed price, while the place can be physical or online.
s: Common features: buyer, seller, price
Differences: face to face against online and delivery
Conclusion about the essential features of a market

questions.q: Nuniz wrote that Hampi was a 'barren' country, yet there was an abundance of everything in its bazaar, and he called it a mystery. Suggest one possible explanation for how the goods came to be there, and say what this suggests about the importance of markets.
questions.a: This is an inference, since the chapter calls it a mystery. Possible explanations: the goods were brought in from elsewhere through trade, or the craftsmen in the streets made them from materials bought in the market. Either way, the chapter says markets help people get goods they cannot create themselves, so the market made the abundance possible. Accept any reasoned explanation.
s: Offers a reasoned explanation (trade or local craftsmen) and treats it as an inference
Links to people needing goods they cannot produce themselves
Concludes the market made the abundance possible

questions.q: A seller bought 100 kg of guavas at Rs 35 per kg and spends Rs 700 more that day on carrying them and running his stall. If he sells all 100 kg, the least price per kg at which he avoids a loss is Rs ___.

Mahesh bought tomatoes at Rs 35 per kg. Buyers keep walking away at Rs 60 per kg, but at Rs 45 per kg his stock sold out. A friend urges him to drop the price to Rs 10 per kg 'so that everyone buys'. What is the main problem with that advice?
o: He would make a loss, as that price is not profitable
At that price buyers would refuse to buy from him at all
At that price the government would fix the price for him
At that price the sale could only take place online
questions.a: The chapter says the seller may not agree to a price that is not profitable for him, and a price that is too low means he loses. Rs 10 is far below his cost of Rs 35. Buyers would gladly buy at a very low price, so the first distractor reverses the problem.

questions.q:
A guava seller bought at Rs 35 per kg and will not sell below Rs 40 per kg. A buyer is ready to pay at most Rs 45 per kg.
1. A sale at Rs 38 per kg can take place, because it is above the Rs 35 the seller paid.
2. A sale at Rs 42 per kg can take place, because both sides are willing to accept it.
3. A sale at Rs 48 per kg can take place, because the seller would gain more and the buyer will have to agree.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: A price works only if it is acceptable to both sides. Rs 42 lies between the seller's lowest price (Rs 40) and the buyer's highest (Rs 45), so statement 2 is correct. Rs 38 is below what the seller will accept, and Rs 48 is above what the buyer will pay, so statements 1 and 3 are false.

questions.q: True or False? 'If the seller of guavas fixes a very low price, every buyer is happy, so a very low price is also a good price for the market.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A very low price is not profitable for the seller and he may lose money. The chapter's good price is one that is just right: high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. A price that suits one side only does not settle the market.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: a very low price is not profitable for the seller; the price must suit both sides

questions.q: Which of these pieces of information would NOT help a guava seller to judge roughly how many kilograms to bring next Saturday, going by the chapter?
o: The price at which the farmer sold him guavas last season
How many kg were left unsold at the end of each Saturday
How fast his stock sold out at Rs 40 per kg
How many buyers walked away when he asked Rs 80 per kg
questions.a: The chapter says the seller learns from how buyers respond at different prices and so assesses approximately what quantity buyers need. Unsold stock, speed of sale and walk-aways all show buyers' response. What the farmer charged last season shows nothing about how many kilograms buyers need.

questions.q:
For one weekly market, guava sellers and buyers behave as below.
At Rs 60 per kg: sellers offer 200 kg, buyers need 120 kg.
At Rs 40 per kg: sellers offer 150 kg, buyers need 150 kg.
At Rs 30 per kg: sellers offer 90 kg, buyers need 170 kg.
Which price fits the chapter's idea of a price that is just right?
o: Rs 40, where the amount offered matches the amount needed
Rs 60, where sellers earn most on each kilogram
Rs 30, where buyers would need the most guavas
Rs 45, the average of the three prices
questions.a: The chapter says the amount of goods offered by sellers and the amount required by buyers help determine the price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. At Rs 40 the 150 kg offered is exactly what buyers need. At Rs 60 sellers have 80 kg more than buyers want, at Rs 30 buyers are short of 80 kg, and an average is not a price anyone has tested.

questions.q:
Anwar buys guavas from a farmer at Rs 30 per kg. On four Saturdays he brought 100 kg each time and tried a different price. Unsold guavas had to be thrown away.
Saturday 1: price Rs 80 per kg, 10 kg sold.
Saturday 2: price Rs 60 per kg, 35 kg sold.
Saturday 3: price Rs 50 per kg, 70 kg sold.
Saturday 4: price Rs 40 per kg, 100 kg sold.
(a) According to the chapter, what may happen when a seller fixes a very high price, and which Saturday shows it?
(b) What was his profit or loss on Saturday 1, counting the cost of all 100 kg he bought?
(c) What can Anwar learn from how the quantity sold changed as the price fell?
(d) Which price and quantity would you advise for the next Saturday? Justify using the profit he would have made on Saturdays 2, 3 and 4 had he bought only the quantity that sold, and the chapter's idea.
questions.a: (a) Buyers may not buy at a price they find very high; Saturday 1 (Rs 80, only 10 kg sold). (b) Receipts 10 x 80 = Rs 800; cost 100 x 30 = Rs 3,000; loss Rs 2,200. (c) The seller can assess approximately what quantity buyers need and offer that quantity in future. (d) Buying only what sold: Saturday 2 gives 35 x 30 = Rs 1,050; Saturday 3 gives 70 x 20 = Rs 1,400; Saturday 4 gives 100 x 10 = Rs 1,000. So he should price near Rs 50 and offer about 70 kg. A student who prefers Rs 40 to serve more buyers must explain the lower profit.
s: Part (a): buyers may not buy at a very high price; Saturday 1
Part (b): a loss of Rs 2,200
Part (c): the seller assesses the quantity buyers need and offers it in future
Part (d): Rs 1,050, Rs 1,400 and Rs 1,000 compared, with a justified choice

questions.q: For three Saturdays, Sunil's guavas at Rs 40 per kg sold out by noon. Next Saturday he brings more from the farmer. Which idea from the chapter explains his decision?
questions.a: The chapter says the seller learns from how buyers respond and can assess approximately what quantity buyers need, then offer that quantity in the market in future.
o: He judged from sales roughly how much buyers need
He is told by the government how much to stock
He expects buyers to accept any higher price he asks
He wants to become a wholesaler with a godown

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the guava example of the chapter the price settles near Rs 40 per kg, not at Rs 80 or Rs 20.
Reason (R): Over time, the amount of goods offered by the sellers and the amount required by the buyers help determine a price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both come from the chapter. At Rs 80 buyers hesitate and at Rs 20 the seller finds it unprofitable. The price that is just right comes from the amount sellers offer and buyers need, so R explains why it settles near Rs 40.

questions.q: Jaya buys 50 kg of guavas for Rs 1,700 in all. (a) What does she receive if she sells all 50 kg at Rs 40 per kg, and what is her profit? (b) What happens if the buyers will pay only Rs 32 per kg, and what does that show about the price she can accept?
questions.a: (a) 50 x 40 = Rs 2,000, so profit is 2,000 - 1,700 = Rs 300. (b) At Rs 32 she receives 50 x 32 = Rs 1,600, a loss of Rs 100. She cannot accept a price like that, since a price that is too low for the seller means she loses.
s: Part (a): Rs 2,000 received and Rs 300 profit
Part (b): Rs 1,600 means a loss of Rs 100, so such a low price is not acceptable to the seller

questions.q: Four guava deals are being negotiated. In each, the buyer's highest price and the seller's lowest price are given. In which one can a sale take place at a price both accept?
o: Buyer's highest Rs 45; seller's lowest Rs 40
Buyer's highest Rs 28; seller's lowest Rs 33
Buyer's highest Rs 30; seller's lowest Rs 35
Buyer's highest Rs 22; seller's lowest Rs 25
questions.a: A sale needs a price that is not above the buyer's highest and not below the seller's lowest. Only in the first deal do the two overlap, between Rs 40 and Rs 45. In every other deal the buyer's highest price is below the seller's lowest, so no price suits both.

questions.q: A guava seller's lowest acceptable price is Rs 38 per kg and a buyer's highest is Rs 52 per kg. (a) Between which two amounts can a price that both accept lie, and would Rs 36 or Rs 55 be one? (b) The buyer opens at Rs 30 and the seller at Rs 80. Why is it unlikely that the sale is settled at either of these opening prices?
questions.a: (a) Between Rs 38 and Rs 52. Neither Rs 36 (below the seller's lowest) nor Rs 55 (above the buyer's highest) works. (b) Each opening price suits only one side: Rs 30 is below what the seller can accept and Rs 80 is above what the buyer will pay. The chapter says buyer and seller negotiate until a mutually agreeable price is reached.
s: Part (a): Rs 38 to Rs 52, with both Rs 36 and Rs 55 ruled out
Part (b): each opening price suits one side only, so they negotiate to a price both accept

questions.q: A buyer will pay at most Rs 30 per kg for guavas, but the seller has bought them at Rs 35 per kg and says he will not sell below that. Show that no deal can be made, and say what the chapter says about this situation.
questions.a: The buyer's highest price (Rs 30) is Rs 5 below the least the seller can accept (Rs 35), so no price is acceptable to both. The chapter says that if buyer and seller cannot reach a price both agree on, the transaction may not take place.
s: Compares Rs 30 and Rs 35, a gap of Rs 5
Concludes no price suits both
Links to the chapter: no agreed price, no transaction

questions.q: At Rs 40 per kg a seller is ready to sell 120 kg of guavas, but buyers are ready to buy only 90 kg at that price. (a) Which figure is the supply and which is the demand, by the chapter's meanings? (b) What can the seller do next time, and why?
questions.a: (a) 120 kg is the supply (what sellers are willing and able to sell at that price); 90 kg is the demand (what consumers are willing and able to buy at that price). (b) Sellers offer more than buyers want, so he can bring about 90 kg next time, since he can assess from the buyers' response roughly what quantity they need.
s: Part (a): 120 kg as supply and 90 kg as demand
Part (b): bring about the quantity buyers need, judged from their response

questions.q: Onions are an important part of Indian cooking. In some seasons their supply to the market falls, and in some a very large crop arrives. Using the chapter's idea that price comes from the amount sellers offer and buyers need, reason out what is likely to happen to the price in each case, and say why the seller cannot fix any price he likes.
questions.a: When supply falls and buyers still need onions, there is less to go around, so the price is likely to rise. When a very large crop arrives and buyers need only so much, sellers have more than buyers need, so the price is likely to fall. This is an inference from the chapter's idea. The seller cannot fix any price he likes because buyers may not buy at a very high price, and a very low price would not be profitable for him; the price has to be acceptable to both.
s: Fall in supply and the likely rise in price
Very large supply and the likely fall in price
Ties each to amount offered against amount needed
Very high price: buyers may not buy
Very low price: not profitable for the seller

questions.q: Ritu says, 'If the buyer will not go above Rs 30 for a kilogram of guavas and the seller will not go below Rs 80, the sale may simply not happen.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, fully. The chapter says that if the buyer and the seller do not reach a price they both agree on, the transaction may not take place. Here neither side moves from its price and the gap between them is Rs 50, so no price suits both. A sale would happen only if one or both sides move.
s: Verdict: agrees fully
Uses the chapter: no agreed price, so the transaction may not take place
Notes that one or both sides would have to move for a sale

questions.q: A roadside stall sells mangoes at Rs 90 per kg and refuses to bargain, saying a lower price would be a loss. A family instead pays Rs 130 per kg for mangoes sold in a neat sealed box at a shopping mall. Give two reasons, not connected to price, for the family's choice.
questions.a: Any two sensible reasons, such as the mangoes are neatly packed and clean, there is no bargaining or argument, everything can be picked up at one place, or they trust the quality of the shop. Price is not the only factor in buying and selling.
s: First valid non-price reason
Second valid non-price reason

questions.q:
A shop in Shimla bought 100 woollen sweaters at Rs 600 each. It sold them in three stages.
November-December: price Rs 1,000, 40 sweaters sold.
January: price Rs 800, 35 sweaters sold.
Late February, when winter was ending: price Rs 550, the last 25 sweaters sold.
(a) Why do garment shops give heavy discounts on woollen clothing at the end of winter? Give a likely reason.
(b) The chapter says a seller may refuse a price that is not profitable. Work out the loss per sweater and in all at the late-February price, and say why the shop accepted it.
(c) Work out the profit earned at each of the first two stages and the total profit on all 100 sweaters.
(d) Before the late-February sale, the owner wondered whether to store the last 25 sweaters and sell them next winter at Rs 1,000 each. Give one point for and one against, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Likely reason (the chapter leaves it as a question): buyers' need for woollens falls once winter is over, so the shop lowers the price to sell what is left. (b) Rs 600 - Rs 550 = Rs 50 per sweater; 25 x 50 = Rs 1,250 in all. The shop accepted it because few buyers now want woollens at a higher price, and the other choice is stock that earns nothing now. (c) November-December: 40 x 400 = Rs 16,000; January: 35 x 200 = Rs 7,000; total = 16,000 + 7,000 - 1,250 = Rs 21,750. (d) For: selling at Rs 550 is below cost, so waiting could bring a better price when buyers need woollens again. Against: the shop holds stock with no money coming in, and buyers' need has fallen, so it may not find buyers soon.
s: Part (a): fall in buyers' need after winter, so the price is cut
Part (b): Rs 50 per sweater, Rs 1,250 in all, and the reason it accepted
Part (c): Rs 16,000, Rs 7,000 and Rs 21,750 in all
Part (d): one point for and one against, linked to buyers' need after winter

questions.q: Write a four-line dialogue between a buyer and a seller of mangoes in which the seller's first price is brought down to a price both accept. Mention the first price, the counter-offer and the final price.
questions.a: Any dialogue with the seller's first price, the buyer's lower counter-offer, and a final price in between at which the sale happens, e.g. Rs 120, Rs 90, Rs 100.
s: Seller's first price stated
Buyer's lower counter-offer stated
Final price between the two, with the sale made

questions.q:
A seller buys guavas from a farmer at Rs 30 per kg and has sold 100 kg every Saturday at Rs 40 per kg. Pleased with the profit, he asks the farmer for 150 kg next Saturday at the same Rs 30. Buyers actually need about 110 kg at Rs 40.
(a) What is his weekly profit on 100 kg?
(b) What would his profit be if all 150 kg sold at Rs 40?
(c) What is his result if only 110 kg sell at Rs 40, with the rest wasted?
(d) Which idea from the chapter did he forget, and what should he do before ordering again?
(e) How may the farmer's thinking about next season change after this?
questions.a: (a) 100 x 40 - 100 x 30 = 4,000 - 3,000 = Rs 1,000. (b) 150 x 40 - 150 x 30 = 6,000 - 4,500 = Rs 1,500. (c) 110 x 40 = 4,400 received against 4,500 spent: a loss of Rs 100. (d) The seller must assess approximately what quantity buyers need from their response and offer that quantity; more guavas than buyers need earn nothing. He should order near what sold out and test before raising it. (e) This is an inference from the chapter's idea: the farmer too will watch how much buyers need, and not simply grow more because one buyer wants more, since the amount offered and the amount needed together decide the price.
s: Part (a): Rs 1,000
Part (b): Rs 1,500 if all sold
Part (c): a loss of Rs 100 on 110 kg sold
Part (d): assess the quantity buyers need and offer that quantity
Part (e): the farmer would think about the demand, marked as an inference

questions.q: Seema's father wants to buy a television and prefers to see it before paying; her mother prefers to order it on a shopping app. (a) Give one point from the chapter that supports each parent. (b) For which would the choice of an online market be worse: the television or a blouse that Seema's tailor must stitch to her measurements? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Father: in a physical market the buyer can meet the seller physically. Mother: on an app, goods such as TVs are delivered to the doorstep and the buyer need not travel. (b) The blouse: tailoring needs in-person contact and cannot be provided online.
s: Part (a): one point for each parent from the chapter
Part (b): the blouse, because tailoring needs in-person contact

questions.q: A Tirupur company orders cotton yarn on a shopping website and uses it to make T-shirts that it sells to shops. Which pairing is correct in the chapter's terms?
o: The yarn is an input for production; the company a manufacturer
The yarn is a finished good for it; the company is an aggregator
The yarn is an export for it; the company is a distributor
The yarn is an input for production; the company is an importer
questions.a: Materials used to make goods are inputs for production, and a person or company that makes goods for sale is a manufacturer. The website, not the company, is the aggregator, and nothing in the case crosses a border, so import or export does not arise.

questions.q:
A Kochi food company buys palm oil each quarter. Its orders were: Malaysia 2,400 tonnes at Rs 90,000 per tonne; Indonesia 3,600 tonnes at Rs 88,000 per tonne; Thailand 1,000 tonnes at Rs 95,000 per tonne. The company also sells packed biscuits to a shop in Dubai. A Kerala supplier now offers palm oil at Rs 94,000 per tonne.
(a) Are the three orders in a domestic or an international market, and what term describes the company's role as buyer?
(b) What term describes the sale of biscuits to Dubai from the company's side?
(c) What did the Indonesian order cost, in crore rupees?
(d) For next quarter's 3,600 tonnes, should the company buy from Indonesia or from the Kerala supplier? Decide, using the price difference and one point about domestic and international markets.
questions.a: (a) International market; the company is an importer (it imports palm oil). (b) Export. (c) 3,600 x 88,000 = Rs 31,68,00,000 = Rs 31.68 crore. (d) Indonesia is Rs 6,000 per tonne cheaper, so 3,600 x 6,000 = Rs 2.16 crore less. Either choice can be argued: Indonesia saves money; the Kerala supplier keeps the trade inside India's boundaries (a domestic market) with no import across a border. This is a judgement; the chapter says only that most palm oil is imported from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
s: Part (a): international market; import
Part (b): export
Part (c): Rs 31.68 crore
Part (d): a decision using the Rs 2.16 crore difference and a point on domestic or international markets

questions.q: A school needs 20 benches. An online seller lists them at Rs 1,800 each with Rs 600 delivery for the whole order. The local timber market sells the same benches at Rs 1,900 each, with no delivery charge. Which statement is correct?
o: Buying online costs Rs 36,600 and saves Rs 1,400
Buying online costs Rs 36,000 and saves Rs 2,000
Buying online costs Rs 37,200 and saves Rs 800
The two cost the same, because delivery cancels the lower price
questions.a: Online: 20 x 1,800 = Rs 36,000 plus Rs 600 delivery = Rs 36,600. Local: 20 x 1,900 = Rs 38,000. The saving is Rs 1,400. The other options leave out the delivery charge or add it twice. The chapter notes that online goods are delivered to the doorstep, but the delivery has a cost.

questions.q: Karan says, 'When a Surat saree maker sells sarees to a shop in Jaipur, it is an export, because the sarees leave Surat.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter's meaning of export.
questions.a: Not at all. Export means selling goods or services produced in one country to a buyer in another country. Jaipur is inside India, so the sale takes place within the boundaries of the country and is a domestic market transaction. Leaving a city is not the same as crossing a country's border.
s: Verdict: disagrees entirely
Meaning of export: sale to a buyer in another country
Jaipur is inside India, so the sale is domestic

questions.q: A Surat saree maker sells 900 sarees at Rs 1,500 each to a shop in Jaipur and 600 sarees at Rs 2,000 each to a shop in Dubai. Her earnings from exports are Rs ___ lakh.
True or False? 'Online classes can be taken without leaving home, so every service can be moved from a physical market to an online market.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says some services, such as tailoring, need in-person contact and cannot be provided online. Online classes are one example of a service that can be bought online, but they do not make every service suitable.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: services needing in-person contact, like tailoring, cannot be provided online

questions.q:
A family lives in a village 30 km from a town. A bus round trip costs Rs 100 for one person. Each month they need groceries and books, which cost the same online as in town, and one blouse stitched by a tailor in town who must take measurements. An online order carries Rs 80 delivery. They plan one order a month.
(a) Which of their needs can an online market meet and which cannot, according to the chapter?
(b) What do they spend on travel and delivery in a month if they buy the groceries and books online but still go to town for the blouse?
(c) What do they spend if they do everything in town?
(d) In which situation would ordering online save money, and by how much?
(e) Advise the family and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Groceries and books can be bought online and delivered to the doorstep; the stitching needs in-person contact and cannot be provided online. (b) The trip to town for the blouse costs Rs 100 and delivery Rs 80, so Rs 180. (c) Rs 100 for one trip. (d) If they had no tailoring and no other reason to go to town, ordering online costs Rs 80 against Rs 100 for the trip, saving Rs 20. (e) As long as the blouse needs a monthly trip, they should shop in town on that trip (Rs 100 against Rs 180); online buying pays only when no trip is needed, or when the delivery saves more than the Rs 100 trip. A reasoned recommendation is accepted.
s: Part (a): goods online, tailoring in person
Part (b): Rs 180
Part (c): Rs 100
Part (d): Rs 20 saving when no trip is needed
Part (e): a recommendation based on the figures and the tailoring limit

questions.q: Gauri says, 'The share market is not really a market, because nobody buys or sells goods or services there.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: It is a market of another kind, one the chapter says does not transact goods and services
She is right, because the chapter says every market must sell goods
She is right, because the chapter treats it as a domestic market only
It is a physical market like a haat, because buyers and sellers meet there
questions.a: The chapter names the share or stock market as one of the other types of markets that do not transact goods and services. So being a market does not depend on selling goods. The other options make claims that the chapter does not.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The paper used to print the Class 7 textbook was bought in a domestic market.
Reason (R): Domestic markets exist outside a nation's boundary.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: the paper came from big paper mills located all over India, so buyer and seller were inside the country. R is false: a domestic market is within the geographical boundaries of the country, and it is international markets that exist outside a nation's boundary.

questions.q: A Pune family orders a pair of shoes on an app from a seller in Agra. 'Physical or online' and 'domestic or international' are two different ways of sorting markets. (a) Sort this purchase on both scales. (b) Could the same shoes be bought in a physical, domestic market? Say what would change.
questions.a: (a) Online (bought through an app, delivered) and domestic (buyer and seller are both inside India). (b) Yes: if the family bought them in a shop or mall in Pune, it would be a physical market, still domestic. The buyer would meet the seller and carry the shoes home instead of having them delivered.
s: Part (a): online and domestic
Part (b): physical but still domestic, with the buyer meeting the seller

questions.q: Show that the statement 'every market is a place where goods or services are bought and sold' cannot be true, using a market named in the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter names the share or stock market as a market that does not transact goods and services. So at least one market exists in which goods or services are not bought and sold, and the statement fails. The weekly haat, where vegetables are sold, fits the statement, but one exception is enough to show it cannot hold for every market.
s: Names the share or stock market
States it does not transact goods and services
Concludes that one exception is enough to disprove 'every'

questions.q:
Read the statements about markets.
1. A weekly haat is a physical market, but a mall, being a building with many stores, is an online market.
2. Manufacturers can buy components online to be used as inputs for production.
3. The share or stock market is a market, but it does not transact goods and services.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: malls, multi-storey buildings with stores inside, are physical markets, like weekly markets and haats.

questions.q:
The library of a Nagpur school needs 60 copies of a reading book before its Reading Week begins in 10 days. A local bookshop offers them at Rs 240 each, ready to collect today. A shopping app run by an aggregator offers Rs 210 each plus Rs 450 for delivery of the whole order, with delivery promised in 8 days.
(a) Which offer is in a physical market and which in an online market? State how the books reach the school in each.
(b) The app is run by an aggregator. Using the chapter's meaning of the word, say what an aggregator does that the single local bookshop does not.
(c) How much would the library save by using the app?
(d) Choose between the two and justify, using one point about money and one about the nature of the physical or online market.
questions.a: (a) The bookshop is a physical market: the school collects the books in person. The app is an online market: the books are delivered to the doorstep. (b) An aggregator is a website or mobile application that organises and combines offers from multiple sellers and sells them to consumers at one place; the local bookshop offers only its own stock. (c) Bookshop 60 x 240 = Rs 14,400; app 60 x 210 + 450 = Rs 13,050; saving Rs 1,350. (d) Either may be defended: the app saves Rs 1,350 and delivers to the doorstep, but delivery leaves only 2 days of margin; the bookshop costs more but the books can be checked in person and collected today, so there is no risk of delay.
s: Part (a): bookshop physical, collected in person; app online, doorstep delivery
Part (b): aggregator combines offers from many sellers at one place, unlike the single bookshop
Part (c): Rs 1,350 saved
Part (d): a choice backed by the saving and the physical or online nature of the market

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term in Column B that describes it.
Column A: 1. A customer picks a pair of shoes from a store inside a city mall  2. A TV ordered on a phone is delivered to the buyer's door  3. A Delhi company sells software services to a client in Canada  4. A Chennai company buys palm oil from Indonesia
Column B: a. an import for the buyer  b. an export for the seller  c. a physical market  d. an online market
questions.a: A mall store is a physical market; an order on a phone delivered to the door is an online market; selling services to a buyer in another country is an export; buying palm oil from Indonesia is an import. The wrong pairings swap import with export or physical with online.

questions.q: A buyer can order 4 books online at Rs 125 each with a delivery charge of Rs 60 for the order, or buy them from the local bookshop at Rs 140 each with no delivery charge. (a) Work out the total in each case. (b) Give one reason, other than money, why the buyer might choose each market.
questions.a: (a) Online: 4 x 125 + 60 = Rs 560. Local: 4 x 140 = Rs 560. The totals are equal. (b) Online: the books come to the doorstep and the buyer need not travel. Local shop: the buyer can meet the seller and see the books before paying.
s: Part (a): Rs 560 in each case, so no money difference
Part (b): one non-money reason for online and one for the physical shop

questions.q: Write a short situation, in three or four sentences, in which a customer cannot be served by an online market even though the seller has a good app. Name the service, say why it cannot be given online and say where the customer must go instead.
questions.a: Any suitable situation, e.g. a customer wants a school uniform stitched to her measurements. Tailoring needs in-person contact, so it cannot be provided online, and she must go to a physical market, the tailor's shop. The service must be one needing in-person contact.
s: A service needing in-person contact named
Reason: it needs in-person contact, so cannot be given online
The customer goes to a physical market

questions.q: A printing press in Pune buys its paper from a mill in Odisha, and a Chennai company buys palm oil from Indonesia. Which description is correct?
questions.a: The paper deal is inside India, so it is in the domestic market, like the paper for printing the book. Buying palm oil from Indonesia crosses the border, so it is an import in an international market.
o: Paper: domestic market; palm oil: import
Paper: import; palm oil: domestic market
Paper: export; palm oil: import
Paper and palm oil: both domestic markets

questions.q:
A student writes, 'India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils in 2024, so India must have no domestic market for vegetable oils.' Using the chapter, decide whether the conclusion follows.
(a) Explain domestic and international markets and import.
(b) State what the chapter says about India's vegetable oil imports.
(c) Say whether any of this shows that there is no domestic market, and what the student would need to know.
questions.a: (a) A domestic market is within the geographical boundaries of the country, as when paper for this book was bought from mills located all over India. An international market lies outside a nation's boundary: sellers export and buyers import, so trade crosses borders. An import is buying goods or services from another country and bringing them into one's own country. (b) India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils like palm, sunflower and soybean oil in 2024, and most of the palm oil is imported from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. (c) The conclusion does not follow. Being the largest importer says India buys a great deal from abroad; it does not say how much is bought inside India or that no oil is. The chapter gives no figure for oil bought inside India, so the student would need that figure before concluding anything.
s: Domestic market defined with the paper example
International market with import and export defined
The 2024 largest-importer fact and the three palm-oil sources
States that the conclusion does not follow
Says what extra information is needed, since the chapter gives no domestic figure

questions.q: Wasim sells handicrafts from a cart at a weekly haat. His sister says he should also list them on a shopping app. (a) Name one thing he would gain and one thing he would give up by moving entirely to the app. (b) Which two market types does his cart at the haat belong to, on the physical-online and the domestic-international scales, if all his buyers live in the same town?
questions.a: (a) Gain: buyers far away can buy from him and goods are delivered to their doors. Give up: the chance to meet buyers face to face at the haat. (b) A physical market and a domestic market, since buyers and seller meet and all lie inside the country.
s: Part (a): one valid gain and one valid loss
Part (b): physical and domestic

questions.q: Ganesh buys rice from farms in large lots and stores it in a godown. Imran runs a corner kirana store that sells 1 kg bags to families from the same area. Which description fits them in the chapter's terms?
o: Ganesh is a wholesaler and Imran is a retailer
Ganesh is a retailer and Imran is a wholesaler
Both are retailers, as both sell the same rice
Ganesh is an aggregator and Imran is a distributor
questions.a: Wholesalers buy in large quantities from producers and store goods in godowns; retailers are the shopkeepers near households who sell small quantities to final consumers for consumption. An aggregator works online and a distributor bridges distance between wholesalers and retailers, which neither man is doing here.

questions.q: A dyeing unit in Surat buys woven fabric at Rs 90 per metre and sells dyed fabric at Rs 130 per metre. In a week it dyes 5,000 metres. (a) In which two markets of the Surat chain does it deal, and in which role in each? (b) How much more does it receive than it spends on the fabric in the week, and what must that amount cover?
questions.a: (a) It is a buyer in the market for woven fabric and a seller in the market for dyed fabric. (b) 5,000 x (130 - 90) = Rs 2,00,000. This has to cover the dyeing work (dyes, wages, power) and leave the unit something to keep.
s: Part (a): buyer in the woven-fabric market, seller in the dyed-fabric market
Part (b): Rs 2,00,000 and the dyeing costs it must cover

questions.q:
Read the statements about the supply of goods.
1. A dyeing unit in Surat buys woven fabric in one market and sells dyed fabric in the next, so cotton passes through several markets before it reaches the final consumer.
2. Retailers buy from wholesalers mainly so that they can resell the goods to other retailers.
3. In an online market, the aggregator hands each order to a wholesaler, who then delivers it to the buyer.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
questions.a: Only statement 1 is in the chapter: the product moves from one stage to another through markets for woven fabric, dyed fabric and finished products. Statement 2 is false: retailers sell in smaller quantities and the goods are meant for consumption. Statement 3 is false: the aggregator itself packs the products and delivers them to the online buyer.

questions.q: A Surat wholesaler holds 6,000 saree pieces. Forty-five retailers each ask for 140 pieces. Show by calculation that the wholesaler cannot meet every order, and say what the chapter suggests wholesalers do to avoid such a gap.
questions.a: 45 x 140 = 6,300 pieces are wanted but only 6,000 are held, so 300 pieces are short. The chapter says wholesalers assess how much product retailers need, which helps maintain stock with the manufacturers and ensures uninterrupted supply.
s: Total demanded: 6,300
Shortage of 300 pieces
Wholesalers assess retailers' requirements to keep stock

questions.q: A retailer buys tomatoes at Rs 18 per kg and sells them at Rs 25 per kg. His shop costs him Rs 700 on a day. To cover that cost from the difference between his buying and selling prices he must sell at least ___ kg.

A hill-village shopkeeper says, 'We do not need wholesalers. Manufacturers should send goods straight to every shop.' Use the chapter to evaluate this.
(a) What do wholesalers do in a physical market?
(b) What do wholesalers in Surat do that helps the manufacturers?
(c) Where does the chapter show goods going from the manufacturer to a seller without a wholesaler, and who takes over the next stage there?
(d) Give your verdict for the village shops.
questions.a: (a) Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers or manufacturers, store them in godowns (with cold storage for perishables) and supply the shops near households. (b) They assess how much product retailers need, which helps maintain the stock of products with the manufacturers and ensures an uninterrupted supply to consumers. (c) In online markets, manufacturers send bulk quantities to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator packs and delivers. (d) A reasoned verdict: for scattered shops in hills, the chapter says even wholesalers find it hard to reach many retailers because of distance and terrain, so distributors are needed; a manufacturer sending goods to every shop would meet the same difficulty without the wholesaler's storage and stock assessment. Direct supply can work only where something like an aggregator handles the packing and delivery.
s: Part (a): bulk buying, storage in godowns, supply to shops
Part (b): assessing retailers' needs to keep stock with manufacturers
Part (c): the online chain, with the aggregator packing and delivering
Part (d): a verdict with at least one reason from the chapter

questions.q: A wholesaler buys 500 kg of tomatoes at Rs 12 per kg and holds them for three days in an ordinary godown. 40 kg rot. He sells the rest to retailers at Rs 18 per kg. What is his profit on this lot?
questions.a: He paid 500 x 12 = Rs 6,000. He sells 460 kg at Rs 18 = Rs 8,280, so the profit is Rs 2,280. Rs 3,000 ignores the rotten tomatoes, Rs 2,760 forgets that he paid for the 40 kg that rotted, and Rs 8,280 is the money received, not the profit. The chapter says warehouses for perishables may have cold storage to avoid this.

questions.q:
A group of farmers near Nashik has 500 kg of tomatoes this week. The wholesaler buys from farmers at Rs 9 per kg and sells to retailers at Rs 18 per kg, and the retailers sell to consumers at Rs 25 per kg. A weekly market in town will buy up to 300 kg at Rs 22 per kg, but the group must pay Rs 3,200 for the stall, transport and a person's time. In Plan 2 the group takes the stall, sells what the market buys at Rs 22 and sells the remainder to the wholesaler at Rs 9. In Plan 3 it sells all 500 kg to the wholesaler.
(a) Name the two links between the farmers and the final consumers, and work out what per cent of the consumer's Rs 25 the farmer gets when he sells to the wholesaler.
(b) Why does the wholesaler need a facility mentioned in the chapter if retailers do not buy at once, and which facility is it?
(c) Work out the money the group keeps in Plan 2 if the market buys the full 300 kg, and in Plan 3.
(d) Work out the least number of kg the market must buy for Plan 2 to be at least as good as Plan 3, and decide which plan to follow if the group is unsure that 300 kg will sell.
questions.a: (a) The wholesaler and the retailer; 9/25 = 36 per cent. (b) Tomatoes are perishable; the chapter says warehouses for perishables may have cold storage facilities at low temperatures, so the wholesaler can hold the stock without loss. (c) Plan 2: 300 x 22 = 6,600 less 3,200 = 3,400, plus 200 x 9 = 1,800, so Rs 5,200. Plan 3: 500 x 9 = Rs 4,500. (d) With k kg sold at the market, Plan 2 keeps 22k - 3,200 + 9(500 - k) = 13k + 1,300. This is at least 4,500 when 13k is at least 3,200, so k is at least 246.2, i.e. 247 kg. Plan 2 pays Rs 700 more if all 300 kg sell, but it falls behind Plan 3 below 247 kg and carries the stall work; if the group is unsure about demand, Plan 3 is the safer choice. Either can be defended with the figures.
s: Part (a): wholesaler and retailer; 36 per cent
Part (b): perishable tomatoes need cold storage in the warehouse
Part (c): Rs 5,200 for Plan 2 and Rs 4,500 for Plan 3
Part (d): 247 kg break-even and a decision weighing Rs 700 gain against risk

questions.q: A shopkeeper buys rice from a wholesaler in 50 kg sacks at Rs 1,900 a sack and sells it to families in 1 kg bags at Rs 42 per kg. (a) For which sack or bag is the rice bought for resale and for which for consumption? (b) How much more does he receive for the rice of one sack than he paid for it?
questions.a: (a) The shopkeeper buys the sack to sell on to families; the family buys the 1 kg bag for consumption. (b) 50 x 42 = Rs 2,100 received against Rs 1,900 paid, so Rs 200 more.
s: Part (a): sack for resale by the retailer, bag for consumption by the family
Part (b): Rs 2,100 less Rs 1,900 = Rs 200

questions.q:
Match each problem in Column A with what the chapter offers to meet it, in Column B.
Column A: 1. A grape wholesaler fears spoilage while waiting for buyers  2. A wholesaler cannot reach many shops spread over rough terrain  3. A manufacturer wants buyers across the country to find its goods at one place on a phone  4. Families need small quantities of goods close to their homes
Column B: a. a distributor  b. an aggregator  c. a retailer  d. cold storage in the warehouse
questions.a: Perishables need cold storage; distributors bridge the gap created by distances and terrain; an aggregator combines the offers of many sellers at one place online; retailers sell small quantities near households. The wrong pairings swap distributor with aggregator or retailer with aggregator.

questions.q: Farmers in a district throw away tomatoes during a bumper harvest because retailers are not buying that week. (a) Give one way in which a wholesaler with cold storage can reduce the waste. (b) Why can the wholesaler not simply buy every tomato at any price the farmers ask?
questions.a: (a) The wholesaler buys in large quantities and stores the tomatoes in cold storage at low temperatures, so they do not spoil while waiting for retailers. (b) The wholesaler must be able to sell on at a price that is profitable; if the price he pays is too high, he would make a loss, and a seller does not agree to a price that is not profitable for him. Any sensible version is accepted.
s: Part (a): bulk purchase and cold storage so the produce keeps
Part (b): he must be able to sell on profitably

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A distributor may be needed between a wholesaler and the small shops of a hill region.
Reason (R): Distances and terrain make it difficult for wholesalers to reach a large number of retailers.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are in the chapter. The reason why a distributor is needed is exactly that distance and terrain make it hard for wholesalers to reach many retailers, so R explains A.

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'In an online order, the manufacturer sends bulk goods to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator then passes each order to a wholesaler, who delivers it to the buyer.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The first half is right: manufacturers send bulk quantities to the warehouse of the business that sells through the app, the aggregator. The second half is wrong: the aggregator itself packs the products and delivers them to the online buyer, and the chapter names no wholesaler at that stage.
s: Verdict: agrees only partly
Accepts that bulk goods go from the manufacturer to the aggregator's warehouse
Rejects the wholesaler's delivery: the aggregator packs and delivers

questions.q: A wholesaler's godown holds sacks of wheat, crates of grapes, boxes of chemicals and cartons of vehicle parts. Which of these would the chapter lead him to keep in a warehouse with cold storage while waiting for orders?
o: The crates of grapes
The sacks of wheat
The boxes of chemicals
The cartons of vehicle parts
questions.a: The chapter says that for perishables the warehouses may also have cold storage facilities at low temperatures to preserve them. Grapes are perishable; wheat, chemicals and vehicle parts are stored in ordinary godowns or specialised warehouses.

questions.q: Compare how goods reach the buyer in a physical market and in an online market. Analyse which links are common and which are different, and say why distributors matter in one of them.
questions.a: Physical: producers or manufacturers, wholesalers (godowns, mandis), distributors, retailers and then consumers. Online: manufacturers send bulk goods to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator packs and delivers to the consumer. Common: producers at the start and the consumer at the end. Different: in the online chain the aggregator handles the stages after the manufacturer, receiving bulk goods, packing and delivering to the doorstep; the chapter does not name a wholesaler or retailer in that chain. Distributors matter in the physical chain because distance and terrain make it hard for wholesalers to reach many retailers; they bridge the gap.
s: Physical chain stages
Online chain stages
Common links
The aggregator and doorstep delivery as the difference
Distributors bridging distance and terrain

questions.q: The chapter says Surat's location on the west coast led to the setting up of ports and road networks that continue to be important today. (a) Name the two facilities linked with the location. (b) Explain how one of them helps a Surat wholesaler who supplies shops across the country and abroad.
questions.a: (a) Ports and road networks. (b) For example, roads let the wholesaler send fabric to shops across the country, and ports let finished goods go abroad; either way, the wholesaler can reach many retailers. The explanation is an inference from the chapter's description of the wholesaler's role.
s: Part (a): ports and road networks
Part (b): a reasoned link to supply across the country or abroad

questions.q: A wholesaler tells a customer, 'We sell to the shops near homes and to the final consumers who shop there.' Which part of this does the chapter contradict?
o: Wholesalers supply goods to the retailers; it is the retailers who sell to final consumers
Wholesalers store goods in godowns before selling them
Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers
Wholesalers supply goods to shops and stores near households
questions.a: The chapter says wholesalers buy in large quantities from producers and supply goods to the shops near households, the retailers; retailers sell to final consumers. So the claim that the wholesaler sells directly to final consumers is the wrong part. The other three statements agree with the chapter.

questions.q: Take any packaged food item you like. Write a flow of goods from the producer to you in at least four stages, naming the role at each stage.
questions.a: Any valid chain, e.g. wheat farmer (producer) - flour mill (manufacturer) - wholesaler (godown) - distributor - retailer (grocery store) - consumer; each stage correctly named with its role.
s: Four or more stages in a sensible order
Each stage named with the role it plays
Ends with the retailer selling to the consumer

questions.q: True or False? 'A salon can be a retail store even though it sells a service and not goods that a customer carries home.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says retail stores also exist for services like salons, movie theatres and restaurants. Retailers sell to final consumers in smaller quantities, and what makes a seller a retailer is serving final consumers near households, not whether the product is a good or a service.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: retail stores exist for services such as salons; retailers serve final consumers

questions.q:
A grape wholesaler in Nashik stores 20 tonnes (20,000 kg) of grapes worth Rs 60 per kg. Assume that without cold storage 15 per cent of the grapes spoil in 5 days and 5 per cent in 2 days. With cold storage only 3 per cent spoil in either period, but the cold store charges Rs 25,000 per day.
(a) What name does the chapter give to goods such as grapes that spoil quickly, and what facility may a warehouse for them have?
(b) What is the value of the grapes that spoil in 5 days without cold storage, and which link in the chain, the farmer or the wholesaler, bears this loss?
(c) What is the total cost of cold storage for 5 days, counting the rent and the value of the grapes that still spoil?
(d) The buyers from the mandi will collect the grapes in just 2 days. Should the wholesaler use cold storage? Decide, with figures.
questions.a: (a) Perishables; cold storage facilities that keep a low temperature. (b) 15% of 20,000 = 3,000 kg, worth 3,000 x 60 = Rs 1,80,000. The wholesaler bears it, because he has bought the produce from the farm and is holding it in his warehouse. (c) Spoilage 3% = 600 kg = Rs 36,000; rent 5 x 25,000 = Rs 1,25,000; total Rs 1,61,000, which is less than Rs 1,80,000. (d) For 2 days: without cold storage 5% = 1,000 kg = Rs 60,000; with it 36,000 + 2 x 25,000 = Rs 86,000. So for only 2 days cold storage costs more, and the wholesaler need not use it; it pays only when produce must be kept longer.
s: Part (a): perishables; cold storage
Part (b): Rs 1,80,000 and the wholesaler as the link holding the loss
Part (d): no cold storage for 2 days, as Rs 86,000 exceeds Rs 60,000

questions.q: Ravi says, 'A market helps only the sellers. If all the markets in town closed, buyers would lose nothing, because they could make whatever they need at home.' Which statement from the chapter weakens his claim most directly?
o: Markets help individuals, households and businesses get goods and services they need but cannot produce themselves
Markets connect people, traditions and ideas
About 3000 women own and run all the shops in Ima Keithal
Sellers of haldi and kumkum in south India give a little free to each buyer
questions.a: Ravi claims that buyers can make everything themselves. The chapter says markets give access to goods and services that people need and cannot produce themselves, which answers him directly. The other statements are true in the chapter but are about connection, a particular market or a custom, and do not address what buyers would lose.

questions.q: Classify each of the following as an economic or a non-economic significance of markets, using the chapter: (i) a cloth producer buys cotton, (ii) a family keeps a monthly account with its grocer for 30 years, (iii) a seller in south India gives a little haldi and kumkum free to each buyer, (iv) a trader in Ima Keithal earns an income. (b) Why does the chapter still call the economic role the primary one?
questions.a: (a) Economic: (i) and (iv). Non-economic: (ii) and (iii). (b) The chapter says the primary role of the market is to promote economic activities, that is, buying and selling for money; relationships and traditions grow around that exchange and add to it.
s: Part (a): (i) and (iv) economic, (ii) and (iii) non-economic
Part (b): economic activity is the primary role; relationships are an addition

questions.q: A haldi and kumkum seller in Madurai gives every buyer a small pinch of each, free of charge. A classmate says the seller is losing money for nothing. Which reading fits the chapter best?
o: It is a tradition beyond buying and selling, a mark of good wishes
It is a price discount that the government has asked sellers to give
It is a way of fixing the price at its minimum limit
It is a quality mark that shows the haldi is safe to eat
questions.a: The chapter describes sellers of haldi and kumkum in south India giving a small quantity of each at no charge as a mark of auspiciousness and good wishes, a practice that goes beyond just buying and selling. It is not a government rule, a price limit or a certification mark.

questions.q: Many families in a town begin asking shopkeepers for millet biscuits instead of maida biscuits. Trace how this demand can pass along the chain of retailers, wholesalers and producers, and say what the producers do. Which example in the chapter works in the same way?
questions.a: Consumers ask retailers for millet biscuits; retailers order more from wholesalers or distributors; the orders reach the producers, who get an indication of what consumers would buy and make more millet biscuits. The chapter's own example is refrigerators that use less electricity, which benefits society.
s: Consumers' request reaches the retailers
It passes back through wholesalers to the producers, who make more of the product
Names the chapter's energy-efficient refrigerator example

questions.q: A Surat cloth maker needs 2.4 kg of cotton for every 10 metres of cloth. For an order of 5,000 metres she must buy ___ kg of cotton from the market.

Assertion (A): Ima Keithal provides employment and is an important source of income for thousands of families.
Reason (R): Ima Keithal is a melting pot of cultures, where people from different communities exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter. The market gives income because its shops sell vegetables, clothes, handloom and daily essentials to buyers; the mixing of cultures is a separate benefit. R therefore does not explain A.

questions.q:
A town council wants to shift a women's market of 3,000 traders, like Ima Keithal, into a new complex. At present the average trader earns Rs 14,000 a month. In the new complex rents are higher: only 80 per cent of the traders could afford to stay, but those who stay would earn Rs 19,000 a month, because the complex is on a busy road.
(a) The chapter describes two kinds of significance of a market. Name one benefit of Ima Keithal under each.
(b) Compare the total monthly earning of all traders now and after the move, in crore rupees.
(c) How many traders would lose their place, and which of the benefits in (a) is then most at risk?
(d) Should the council accept the plan? Decide, weighing the figures against what the chapter says such a market gives to people.
questions.a: (a) Economic: employment and income for thousands of families. Non-economic: it is a melting pot of cultures where communities exchange ideas and shared traditions. (b) Now 3,000 x 14,000 = Rs 4.2 crore; after the move 2,400 x 19,000 = Rs 4.56 crore, Rs 36 lakh more. (c) 20% of 3,000 = 600 traders lose their place; the income of their families is most at risk, and the mixing of communities may also be reduced if those who cannot afford the rent belong to particular communities. (d) Either decision can be defended. Accept: total earnings rise by Rs 36 lakh and each trader who stays earns Rs 5,000 more. Reject or change: 600 families lose their only market income and the market's role as a meeting place of communities is damaged. The answer must use the figures and the chapter's two roles, and may propose a middle course such as lower rents.
s: Part (a): an economic and a non-economic benefit named
Part (b): Rs 4.2 crore and Rs 4.56 crore
Part (c): 600 traders; income of their families (and possibly the mixing of communities) at risk
Part (d): a decision weighing the Rs 36 lakh gain against the lost places and the chapter's two roles

questions.q: In one town in a week the numbers are: rice, 40 sellers and 900 buyers; notebooks, 25 sellers and 600 buyers; hand-carved wooden temple models, 2 sellers and 5 buyers; school bags, 30 sellers and 700 buyers. Following the chapter's account of Aakriti's paintings, for which product will a seller find it hardest to know what price buyers will accept?
o: The hand-carved wooden temple models
Rice
Notebooks
School bags
questions.a: Aakriti's difficulty is that there are few local buyers and sellers of her kind of product, so she has little idea where to sell or what price to ask, unlike the guava seller. The temple models, with 2 sellers and 5 buyers, are in the same position. Rice, notebooks and school bags have many buyers and sellers.

questions.q: True or False? 'A family that has stayed with the same tailor for decades is still taking part in the market's economic role, because it pays him for stitching; the trust between them is an addition to that role.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the primary role of the market is to promote economic activities, and that it also has non-economic significance in many people's lives, such as long-lasting trusted relationships with a tailor, jeweller or doctor. The trust is added to the economic exchange, not a replacement for it.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: the economic role continues and the relationship is an added non-economic significance

questions.q: Imagine a town where all markets are closed for a month. Analyse what would happen to farmers, to a cloth producer in a textile city, to a family, and to an artist like Aakriti, using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Farmers could not sell rice, wheat, dal, vegetables and fruits, so they would earn nothing. A cloth producer could not buy cotton as an input, so production would stop. The family could not get goods it cannot produce, such as food, cloth and other needs. Aakriti, who already struggles to find buyers, would have no way to sell. The town would also lose the interactions and traditions that markets carry.
s: Effect on farmers
Effect on the cloth producer
Effect on the family
Effect on the artist
Loss of interaction and traditions

questions.q: A supermarket opens near Mrs Iyer's house and sells rice Rs 2 per kg cheaper. Her family, which has kept a monthly account with the same grocer for 30 years, continues to buy from him. Which reading fits the chapter best?
o: Markets also carry lasting, trusted relationships, which can matter beside price
The government has fixed the grocer's price so that buyers cannot leave him
A market works only when buyers pay the lowest price available
The family treats the grocer as an aggregator of many sellers
questions.a: The chapter says that, besides the primary economic role, markets have non-economic significance: relationships develop between buyers and sellers across generations, such as a family's monthly account with the local grocer. The other readings bring in a rule, a claim about price that the chapter does not make, or a wrongly used term.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the role of markets.
1. When many consumers begin to ask for refrigerators that use less electricity, producers get an indication of what consumers would buy.
2. A family's long-lasting trusted relationship with its tailor is a non-economic significance of markets, in addition to their economic role.
3. About 30,000 women own and run all the shops of Ima Keithal in Imphal.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says about 3000 women own and run the shops of Ima Keithal.

questions.q:
A fan company sells a standard ceiling fan at Rs 2,200, earning a profit of Rs 400 on each, and an energy-saving fan at Rs 3,400, earning Rs 500 on each. Its yearly sales are:
Year 1: standard 8,000, energy-saving 2,000.
Year 2: standard 6,000, energy-saving 4,500.
Year 3: standard 3,500, energy-saving 7,500.
(a) Which idea from the chapter does the shift in sales show, and who else gains from it besides the company?
(b) What was the share of energy-saving fans in the Year 3 sales, in per cent, correct to one decimal place?
(c) What was the company's profit in Year 3 from each model, and in all?
(d) The managers must plan Year 4. Should they stop making the standard fan entirely? Decide with reasons.
questions.a: (a) Consumers' choices guide what producers make: buyers are moving to fans that use less electricity, as with the chapter's refrigerators, and society gains from less electricity being used. (b) 7,500 / 11,000 = 68.2 per cent. (c) Standard 3,500 x 400 = Rs 14,00,000; energy-saving 7,500 x 500 = Rs 37,50,000; total Rs 51,50,000. (d) The rising share is the consumers' signal, so the company should make more energy-saving fans. Still, the standard fan earned Rs 14 lakh in Year 3 and 3,500 buyers chose it, so a reasoned plan is to cut but not end it unless the company is sure those buyers will switch.
s: Part (a): consumers' choices guide producers; society gains
Part (b): 68.2 per cent
Part (d): decision using the rising share and the standard-fan buyers

questions.q: A town divides its market into two walled sections, one for traders of each of two communities, with no common passage. (a) Which role of a market, described through Ima Keithal, is weakened? (b) Does this stop buying and selling? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The role of a melting pot of cultures, where people from different communities come together to exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions. (b) No. Shops can still sell and buyers can still buy, so the economic role continues; what is lost is the mixing, a non-economic significance.
s: Part (a): the melting-pot role, communities meeting and exchanging ideas
Part (b): economic role continues, non-economic mixing is lost

questions.q: In a town, many families begin asking shopkeepers for cloth bags instead of plastic ones. Shopkeepers order more cloth bags from their suppliers. Which idea from the chapter does this show?
questions.a: Consumer demand tells producers what buyers want, and producers respond, just as with refrigerators that use less electricity. The other options describe the government's role, supply chains or price negotiation.
o: Consumers' choices guide producers
The government has fixed a minimum price
The seller is bargaining with the buyer
The bags are an input for production now

questions.q: Neha says, 'The main work of a market is building friendships among people. Buying and selling comes second.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Not at all. The chapter says the primary role of the market is to promote economic activities, which involve monetary exchange. Relationships, such as with a family tailor or a grocer's monthly account, are a non-economic significance in addition to that role, not a replacement for it.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Cites the primary role as economic activity involving monetary exchange
Treats relationships as an added, non-economic significance, with an example
