questions.q: The cotton market of a textile city is shut for a week. (a) What do the cloth producers of the city lose, and what follows for their output? (b) Which later link of the chain feels it next, and how does a family buying a shirt feel it?
questions.a: (a) They lose the input, cotton, which they cannot produce themselves, so they cannot make cloth. (b) Wholesalers and retailers have no cloth to sell, so the family cannot get the shirt cloth, a good it cannot produce itself. The chain is traced by inference from the chapter's description of the network.
s: Part (a): cotton as the input they cannot make, so cloth output stops
Part (b): the next link has no cloth to sell and the family cannot get the shirt

questions.q:
Aakriti paints in oils. At a local fair she can sell about 2 paintings a month at Rs 6,000 each. An app that lists her paintings to buyers in other cities could sell about 8 a month at Rs 5,000 each, but takes a 10 per cent commission on each sale.
(a) Why does Aakriti find it hard to sell and price her paintings locally, according to the chapter?
(b) What does she earn a month at the fair?
(c) What does she keep a month from the app after commission?
(d) How does the chapter's description of an online market explain the larger number of buyers?
(e) Name one thing about the app figures that she cannot be sure of, and advise her.
questions.a: (a) There are fewer local buyers and sellers of artwork, unlike the case of guavas. (b) 2 x 6,000 = Rs 12,000. (c) 8 x 5,000 = 40,000; commission 4,000; she keeps Rs 36,000, which is Rs 24,000 more. (d) On an app buyers and sellers need not meet and may be thousands of kilometres apart, so many more buyers can be reached. (e) The figure of 8 sales a month is an estimate and may not be reached; also the price may be hard to fix for buyers who cannot see the work. A reasoned advice, such as trying the app while keeping the fair, is accepted. If only 3 sold at Rs 5,000, she would keep 13,500, still above Rs 12,000.
s: Part (a): few local buyers and sellers
Part (b): Rs 12,000
Part (c): Rs 36,000 after commission
Part (d): online reaches buyers far away, who need not meet the seller
Part (e): an uncertainty named and a reasoned advice

questions.q: Describe in about four lines a relationship between your family and a shopkeeper, tailor or doctor. Show one economic side and one non-economic side of it.
questions.a: Any suitable account, e.g. 'We have bought books from Sharma Uncle for ten years. We pay for what we take (economic). He remembers our needs and greets my grandmother (relationship and trust).' It must show both sides.
s: A real or realistic buyer-seller relationship described
Economic side: exchange of goods or services for money
Non-economic side: trust, goodwill or tradition

questions.q: (a) Why does Aakriti find it hard to decide the price of her paintings? (b) Suggest one way, other than a local shop, by which an artist can find buyers today.
questions.a: (a) There are fewer local buyers and sellers of artwork, so she has few signs of what price buyers will accept, unlike the guava seller. (b) Sell through an online market such as a website or app, or through a haat or fair (any sensible way).
s: Part (a): few buyers and sellers, so no clear price signal
Part (b): a reasonable way to reach buyers, such as an online market

questions.q: Which of these shows the government ensuring quality and safety standards, as the chapter describes, and not controlling a price?
o: Approving a new medicine through set procedures and testing samples of what is produced
Allowing no lifesaving drug to be sold above a fixed upper limit
Announcing that paddy cannot be sold below a set minimum
Requiring employers to pay workers at least a fixed amount for a day's work
questions.a: The chapter says the government sets procedures for approvals of medicines and conducts sample testing to check that the produced drug meets standards of quality, so there is no risk to consumers' health. The other three are price controls: a maximum price for drugs, a minimum price for paddy and a minimum wage.

questions.q: A factory makes 2 lakh single-use plastic cups a month and earns Rs 0.30 profit on each. The cups clog the town's drains, and the town spends Rs 1,50,000 a month to clear them. (a) Compare the factory's monthly profit with the cost borne by the town. (b) Who bears this cost, and what does the chapter say the government does in such a case?
questions.a: (a) Profit = 2,00,000 x 0.30 = Rs 60,000; the town's cost is Rs 1,50,000, which is Rs 90,000 more. (b) The townspeople, who are not the cup makers and need not be the buyers, bear it. The chapter says the government plays a crucial role in controlling such effects and intervenes with strict regulations to mitigate the negative effects.
s: Part (a): Rs 60,000 profit against Rs 1,50,000 cost
Part (b): the townspeople bear it; the government regulates

questions.q: A state rule says that a contractor must pay every labourer at least Rs 450 for a day's work. Which statement fits the chapter?
o: It is a minimum wage, so that employers make fair payments
It is a maximum price, so that buyers are not overcharged
It is a minimum price for crops, so that farmers do not lose
It is a public good, as the contractor expects no profit from it
questions.a: The chapter says the government sets minimum wages for work done by employees so that employers make fair payments to them. A maximum price protects buyers of essential goods, a minimum price protects farmers' crops, and a public good is something like a park or road.

questions.q:
A new fever tablet is about to be sold. A manufacturer complains that approval procedures and sample testing slow its launch.
(a) What steps does the chapter say the government takes about medicines?
(b) What could go wrong for consumers if there were no sample testing?
(c) How would you reply to the manufacturer?
(d) The chapter also warns about rules. Say what balance the government should keep.
questions.a: (a) It sets procedures for approvals of medicines and conducts sample testing to check whether the produced drug meets standards of quality. (b) A drug that does not meet standards could reach consumers and put their health at risk; the testing is there so that there is no risk to consumers' health. (c) The checks protect the people who take the medicine; a delay is the price of safety, and a tablet that fails does not serve the manufacturer's customers either. (d) The chapter says governments make rules to ensure markets work fairly and consumers are not exploited, but too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function properly. So the checks should be enough to protect health, without piling on needless rules.
s: Part (a): approval procedures and sample testing
Part (b): risk to consumers' health from drugs below standard
Part (c): a reasoned reply to the manufacturer
Part (d): the chapter's warning that too many rules make it difficult for markets to function
Part (d): a balanced conclusion

questions.q: A town spends Rs 12 lakh a year on policing for its 30,000 residents. Policing is a public good, so the cost of providing it works out to Rs ___ per resident per year.

Read the statements about the government's role.
1. A minimum price for paddy is set to protect consumers from being overcharged.
2. Minimum wages are set so that employees make fair payments to employers.
3. Kautilya's Arthashastra told ghee traders to give buyers 1/50 part more to make up for the ghee sticking to the measuring can.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Only statement 3 is from the chapter. Statement 1 reverses the purpose: a minimum price for crops protects farmers from losses. Statement 2 reverses the payers: minimum wages ensure that employers make fair payments to employees.

questions.q: Meera says, 'Producers sell goods to make a profit. Parks, roads and policing are goods on which they do not expect a profit, so the government provides them.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, fully. The chapter says producers make and sell goods and services to make a profit, but there are goods and services, such as public parks, roads and policing, on which they do not expect a profit. So the government provides these public goods and services for the society.
s: Verdict: agrees fully
Producers aim at profit
No profit expected on public goods like parks, roads and policing, so the government provides them

questions.q: A factory making single-use plastic cups pollutes a river and makes nearby residents ill. The state government brings in strict rules for the factory. Which role of the government is this?
questions.a: Pollution and health risks are effects of markets beyond buying and selling, which the government controls through strict regulations. A price limit, a public good or a weights check does not fit.
o: Mitigating the external effects of markets
Setting a maximum price for an essential good
Providing a public good for all citizens
Checking weights and measures of packets

questions.q:
A weights-and-measures inspector weighs five packets marked '1 kg sugar' from each of three shops (in grams).
Shop A: 1000, 995, 1005, 1000, 1000.
Shop B: 980, 975, 990, 985, 970.
Shop C: 940, 950, 945, 955, 960.
Sugar sells at Rs 48 per kg. Shop C sells about 200 such packets a day and Shop B about 1,500.
(a) Which government role from the chapter is the inspector carrying out?
(b) By how many grams, on average, is a packet from Shop C below the label?
(c) What is the value of the sugar that customers fail to receive in a day, at Shop C and at Shop B?
(d) The inspector has time for a full check of only one shop this week. Which should she choose, and what should be done about the others, keeping in mind the chapter's warning about too many rules?
questions.a: (a) Monitoring the weights and measures of packaged products, to check the net quantity in the package. (b) 940 + 950 + 945 + 955 + 960 = 4,750 g, so 250 g short over five packets, 50 g per packet. (c) Shop C: 200 x 50 g = 10 kg, worth 10 x 48 = Rs 480 a day. Shop B: the five packets total 4,900 g, 20 g short on average; 1,500 x 20 g = 30 kg, worth 30 x 48 = Rs 1,440 a day. (d) Shop B first, since its customers lose three times as much sugar a day although each packet is less short; Shop C should also be told to correct its packing soon, and Shop A needs no action. Choosing Shop C for its larger per-packet shortfall is acceptable only if B's larger total loss is considered. The response should be graded, not excessive, since too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function.
s: Part (a): monitoring weights and measures
Part (b): 50 g per packet
Part (c): Rs 480 a day at C and Rs 1,440 a day at B
Part (d): a choice backed by the daily loss, with graded action and the warning about too many rules

questions.q: True or False? 'A town may make strict rules for a single-use plastic cup factory even though every cup is sold only to buyers who want it, because a market can affect people who are neither its buyers nor its sellers.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says markets sometimes have significant effects beyond the selling and buying, for example pollution from factories making single-use plastics, which poses health risks. The government plays a role in controlling such effects, so the buyer's willingness does not settle the matter.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: markets can have effects beyond buyers and sellers, such as pollution, which the government regulates

questions.q: A town has a free public park, an amusement park run by a company that charges tickets, and police patrols on its roads. (a) Which of these are public goods in the chapter's sense? (b) Why would a company not usually supply them, and who steps in?
questions.a: (a) The free public park and the police patrols (policing) are public goods; the ticketed amusement park is sold for a profit. (b) Producers make goods to earn a profit and do not expect to make a profit on parks, roads and policing, so the government provides them.
s: Part (a): free park and policing identified
Part (b): no profit expected by producers, so the government provides them

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Producers supply public goods such as roads and policing because they expect a profit from them.
Reason (R): Producers make and sell goods and services in order to make a profit.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: R is true: producers sell to make a profit. But A is false: the chapter says public goods such as parks, roads and policing are ones on which producers do not expect to make a profit, so the government provides them.

questions.q: An inspector weighs 8 packets of rice, each marked 500 g, and finds that together they weigh 3.76 kg. Show that all eight packets cannot hold what the label says, and name the government role being used.
questions.a: 8 x 500 g = 4,000 g = 4 kg, but the packets weigh only 3.76 kg, which is 240 g less. So they cannot all be full. The government checks the weights and measures of packaged goods to see the net quantity in the package.
s: Computes 4 kg expected
Shows the shortfall of 240 g
Names monitoring weights and measures as the role

questions.q: Mr Kulkarni buys a sealed packet marked 1 kg of rice but finds that it holds only 900 g. Which government role is meant to guard against this?
questions.a: The government monitors the weights and measures of packaged products to check the net quantity in the package. Price limits and public goods do not deal with underweight packs.
o: Monitoring weights and measures of packages
Fixing a minimum price for the farmers' rice
Providing roads for the transport of rice
Regulating the pollution from rice mills

questions.q: The government tests samples of the medicines produced. In one batch, 2 of the 40 strips tested fail the quality standard. (a) What per cent of the sample failed? (b) Why is it not safe to treat the batch as meeting the standard, and what does the chapter say sample testing protects?
questions.a: (a) 2/40 = 5 per cent. (b) The chapter says sample testing checks whether the produced drug meets standards of quality; if strips in the sample fail, other strips of the batch may fail too. The testing is there so that there is no risk to the consumers' health. The point that other strips may also fail is an inference.
s: Part (a): 5 per cent
Part (b): sample failures mean the batch is not shown to meet the standard; testing protects consumers' health

questions.q:
A lifesaving tablet costs the maker Rs 380 per strip, and the maker produces 10,000 strips a month. The government has set a maximum price of Rs 500 per strip. A group of patients wants the limit lowered to Rs 360. A company wants it raised to Rs 900.
(a) What is the maker's monthly profit at Rs 500?
(b) What happens to the maker at Rs 360, and what does the chapter say about producers when a limit is set too low?
(c) What happens to patients at Rs 900, according to the chapter?
(d) Advise the government.
questions.a: (a) (500 - 380) x 10,000 = Rs 12,00,000. (b) At Rs 360 the maker loses Rs 20 per strip, 20 x 10,000 = Rs 2,00,000 a month; the chapter says that if the price is too low, producers do not have any motivation to produce. (c) Patients would pay Rs 400 more per strip than at Rs 500, and the maker's profit would be Rs 520 a strip; the chapter says that if prices are too high, consumers are disadvantaged. (d) Keep a limit that stays above the maker's cost but protects patients, close to the present Rs 500; neither extreme works. A reasoned advice using the figures is accepted.
s: Part (b): loss of Rs 2,00,000 and no motivation to produce
Part (c): consumers disadvantaged at a very high limit
Part (d): advice that keeps the limit above cost without overcharging

questions.q: Which of these fits the chapter's idea of a public good, whose present use does not reduce its availability for future use?
o: A road that thousands of people use every day
A bottle of drinking water given out free at a fair
A packet of medicine distributed in a health camp
A plate of food served at a community meal
questions.a: The chapter describes a public good as a service or commodity accessible to all members of a society whose present use does not diminish its availability for future use; roads, parks and policing are examples. The water, medicine and food are used up when one person has them.

questions.q: Describe a situation in which the government would need to step in to deal with a harm caused by a market. Name the product, the harm and one step the government could take.
questions.a: Any suitable case, e.g. a factory making single-use plastic bags pollutes drains and harms health; the government could bring in strict rules limiting or banning production.
s: A product or market named
The harm to the environment or health
A government step such as a regulation

questions.q:
Sunita grows 4,000 kg of wheat at a cost of Rs 22 per kg. The government's minimum price for wheat is Rs 24 per kg. In a bumper year without such protection the market price would have fallen to Rs 19 per kg. A proposal is made to raise the minimum price to Rs 30 per kg. A family of four uses about 20 kg of wheat a month. Her town has 400 wheat farmers like Sunita, each selling 4,000 kg, and 8,000 families like the one described.
(a) Under which government role in the chapter does a minimum price for wheat come, and whom does it protect?
(b) What would Sunita's loss have been at Rs 19, and what is her profit at Rs 24?
(c) At Rs 30 instead of Rs 24, how much more would each family pay in a year, how much more would all 8,000 families pay, and how much more would all 400 farmers receive?
(d) Should the government raise the minimum price to Rs 30? Decide, using the figures and the chapter's caution about price limits.
questions.a: (a) Controlling prices to protect buyers and sellers; the minimum price protects farmers so that they do not incur losses. (b) At Rs 19: 4,000 x 3 = Rs 12,000 loss. At Rs 24: 4,000 x 2 = Rs 8,000 profit. (c) Each family: 20 x 6 x 12 = Rs 1,440 a year. All 8,000 families: Rs 1,15,20,000. Each farmer gains 4,000 x 6 = Rs 24,000, so 400 farmers gain Rs 96,00,000. (d) Either side can be argued. For: farmers' profit rises from Rs 8,000 to Rs 32,000 and is safer against higher costs. Against: the Rs 24 price already prevents a loss, which is the purpose of the limit; raising it takes Rs 1.152 crore from consumers to give Rs 96 lakh to farmers, and the chapter warns that if prices are too high, consumers are disadvantaged. The answer must use the figures.
s: Part (a): price control; farmers protected
Part (b): loss of Rs 12,000 and profit of Rs 8,000
Part (c): Rs 1,440 per family, Rs 1,15,20,000 for all families and Rs 96,00,000 for all farmers
Part (d): a decision weighing the two totals and the chapter's caution

questions.q: Assume that, in the time of Kautilya's Arthashastra, 1/50 of the ghee in a measure stuck to the measuring can. A trader measures out 500 ml for a buyer. (a) How much ghee sticks, and how much extra does the rule require him to give? (b) Why was this extra quantity required, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) 500 x 1/50 = 10 ml sticks, so the rule requires him to give 10 ml extra. (b) The rule says buyers shall be given 1/50 part more as manasrava to compensate for the reduction in quantity owing to the ghee sticking to the measuring can; it shows rulers protecting consumers long ago.
s: Part (a): 10 ml stuck and 10 ml extra
Part (b): to compensate for the ghee sticking to the can

questions.q:
Read the statements about judging quality.
1. A TV with more BEE stars uses less electricity, so the buyer's electricity bill is lower.
2. A buyer should expect to find the BEE Star rating on a bag of cement.
3. A shopper who buys a brand because friends recommend it is using the reputation of the product, built through word of mouth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: BEE stars appear on items such as TVs, laptops and air conditioners; cement is a construction material, for which the chapter names the ISI mark.

questions.q: Dev picks up a packet of instant noodles. The label shows ingredients, MRP and a best before date, but no FSSAI mark. Which response fits the chapter best?
o: Look for other evidence; the FSSAI mark shows government testing
Treat it as safe, because a best before date shows it was tested
Look for the ISI mark instead, since ISI is the mark for food items
Look for the BEE star rating, which tells the quality of food
questions.a: The chapter says the FSSAI mark indicates that food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume; a best before date and an ingredient list do not show testing. ISI is mainly for appliances, construction materials, tyres and paper, and BEE stars are for energy efficiency.

questions.q: A shopper says, 'This air conditioner has 5 BEE stars, so it must be the safest and best-made one in the shop.' (a) What does the chapter say BEE stars tell a buyer? (b) Which other mark does the chapter name for the quality and safe use of electrical appliances?
questions.a: (a) BEE stars show the energy efficiency of the appliance: higher stars mean it uses less energy and electricity. They do not show how safe or well made it is. (b) The ISI mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards, which ensures quality and that the product is safe to use.
s: Part (a): stars show energy efficiency, not safety or build
Part (b): the ISI mark

questions.q:
Match each shopper's need in Column A with the mark in Column B that the chapter would have the shopper look for.
Column A: 1. A buyer wants the mark that the chapter names for agricultural products such as honey  2. A buyer wants a sign that a packet of gram flour has been tested by the government and is safe  3. A buyer wants to know how much electricity an air conditioner will use  4. A builder wants a sign of quality and safety on a bag of cement
Column B: a. ISI mark  b. BEE Star rating  c. FSSAI logo  d. AGMARK
questions.a: AGMARK is the certification mark for agricultural products such as honey; the FSSAI logo shows food tested and safe; BEE stars show how much electricity an air conditioner uses; the ISI mark appears on construction materials such as cement. The wrong pairings swap AGMARK with FSSAI or ISI with BEE.

questions.q:
A school kitchen wants 20 jars of honey of 500 g each. Three online sellers offer:
Seller X: Rs 300 a jar, shows FSSAI and AGMARK marks, rating 4.1 stars from 850 reviews.
Seller Y: Rs 240 a jar, shows no certification mark, rating 4.8 stars from 9 reviews.
Seller Z: Rs 280 a jar, shows the FSSAI mark only, rating 4.4 stars from 40 reviews.
(a) Whose rating is the least dependable, and why?
(b) Compare Z with X: what extra does X's AGMARK tell a buyer of honey?
(c) How much more would the school pay for 20 jars from X than from Y, and than from Z?
(d) Which seller would you choose for the school kitchen? Decide, giving one point from marks and one from reviews.
questions.a: (a) Seller Y's: the 4.8 stars come from only 9 reviews, and the product shows no certification mark, so there is little to confirm the rating. (b) AGMARK is the certification mark for agricultural products such as honey, so it adds a second confirmation of quality beyond FSSAI's sign that the food has been tested and is safe. (c) X: 20 x 300 = Rs 6,000; Y: 20 x 240 = Rs 4,800, so Rs 1,200 more; Z: 20 x 280 = Rs 5,600, so Rs 400 more. (d) A defensible choice is X: it has both marks and the most reviews, so its rating is more dependable, and food safety matters in a kitchen. Z is acceptable if argued on its lower price with the FSSAI mark. Y is the cheapest but the least supported.
s: Part (a): Y's rating, with only 9 reviews and no mark
Part (b): AGMARK as the mark for agricultural products such as honey
Part (c): Rs 1,200 and Rs 400
Part (d): a choice with one point from marks and one from reviews

questions.q: A seller's page shows 50 reviews, of which 38 praise the product and 12 find fault. The share of reviews that praise the product is ___ per cent.

A shopper who is allergic to nuts picks up a 1 kg packet of gram flour that carries the FSSAI logo. She thinks, 'Tested and safe, so it is safe for me.' Which item on the label should she read to answer her doubt?
o: The allergen declaration
The batch number
The name and address of the manufacturer
The MRP
questions.a: The FSSAI logo shows that the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume in general. A person with an allergy needs the allergen declaration on the label, which is one of the details listed in the chapter. The batch number, manufacturer's address and MRP say nothing about allergens.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'Buy this 5-star TV instead of the 3-star one and you will save Rs 3,000 on electricity every year.' The 3-star TV uses 250 units a year, the 5-star TV uses 150 units a year, and a unit costs Rs 8. Show that his claim cannot be correct. What does the chapter say a higher star rating does to the bill?
questions.a: 3-star bill: 250 x 8 = Rs 2,000. 5-star bill: 150 x 8 = Rs 1,200. The yearly saving is only Rs 800, so Rs 3,000 is impossible. The chapter says more stars mean the appliance uses less electricity, so the bill is smaller, but not by the amount he says.
s: Both yearly bills worked out
Saving of Rs 800 shown to be less than Rs 3,000
Higher stars mean less electricity and a lower bill

questions.q: A school buys an LED television. The box carries a BEE Star rating of 4 stars and an ISI mark. Which statement fits the chapter?
o: The stars show how little electricity it uses, and the ISI mark shows it meets quality and safety standards
Both marks tell only how little electricity the television uses
The stars show the television has been tested for food safety, and the ISI mark shows its energy use
The two marks cannot both appear on one product
questions.a: The chapter says BEE stars on electronic items such as TVs show energy efficiency (more stars, less electricity), while the ISI mark, issued by BIS, is generally present on electrical appliances and ensures quality and that the product is safe to use. Food safety belongs to FSSAI, and nothing in the chapter stops two marks appearing together.

questions.q: True or False? 'A phone cover with hundreds of 5-star online reviews has been tested by a government agency, so it needs no certification mark.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Online reviews and feedback are opinions of other consumers that help a buyer decide whether to buy; they are not a test by a government agency. Certification marks are provided by government agencies and confirm that a product fulfils minimum quality standards.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: reviews come from other consumers, while certification marks come from government agencies

questions.q:
Your parent asks you to buy a 1 kg packet of gram flour. The packet in your hand shows: net quantity 900 g; date of manufacture 20 August 2025; best before 4 months from manufacture; FSSAI logo and licence number; allergen declaration 'may contain mustard'.
(a) Is the packet the size that was asked for? Give the difference.
(b) What is its best before date?
(c) Which label detail shows that the food has been tested by the government?
(d) Your sister is allergic to mustard. Which detail should she read, and what does it tell her?
(e) Decide whether to buy this packet and give two reasons.
questions.a: (a) No. The net quantity is 900 g, which is 100 g less than 1 kg. (b) 20 August 2025 plus 4 months is 20 December 2025. (c) The FSSAI logo and licence number: the symbol indicates that the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume. (d) The allergen declaration, which says it may contain mustard, so it is not suitable for her. (e) A reasoned decision: do not buy it for the 1 kg need, since it holds only 900 g, and not for the sister, because of the mustard; choose another packet or buy extra. If the family has no allergy and is willing to buy two packets, the FSSAI mark and the long best before date support buying.
s: Part (a): 900 g, 100 g short of 1 kg
Part (b): 20 December 2025
Part (c): FSSAI logo and licence number
Part (d): allergen declaration and what it says
Part (e): a decision with two reasons from the label

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An air conditioner with more BEE stars is likely to give a lower electricity bill.
Reason (R): BEE stars show how safe the appliance is to touch and use.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: higher stars indicate that the appliance uses less energy and electricity, so the bill is smaller. R is false: BEE stars indicate energy efficiency; safety and quality of an electrical appliance are shown by the ISI mark.

questions.q: A neighbour praises a brand of pressure cooker, and its page on a shopping app shows 4.7 stars from only 6 reviews. (a) Which two sources of quality information other than certification marks is Mira using? (b) Why might she hesitate to depend on either alone?
questions.a: (a) Word of mouth (the neighbour's recommendation, which builds the product's reputation) and online reviews and feedback from other consumers. (b) Both are opinions of other buyers and are not tested by a government agency; six reviews are also very few, so she may look for a certification mark. Accept any reasoned hesitation.
s: Part (a): word of mouth and online reviews
Part (b): a reasoned limit, such as opinions only or very few reviews

questions.q: Four air conditioners of the same size and price use these units of electricity a year: A 1,400, B 1,150, C 1,000, D 1,250. A unit costs Rs 8. Which one is most likely to carry the most BEE stars, and by how much does its yearly bill fall below A's?
o: C, by Rs 3,200
B, by Rs 2,000
C, by Rs 400
D, by Rs 1,200
questions.a: More BEE stars mean the appliance uses less electricity, so the one using the fewest units, C, is the most likely to have the most stars. A's bill is 1,400 x 8 = Rs 11,200 and C's is 1,000 x 8 = Rs 8,000, a fall of Rs 3,200. Rs 400 is the fall in units, not rupees.

questions.q: A notice board in your colony needs a shopping tip headed 'Look for the mark'. Write three lines, one each for a packet of pulses, a refrigerator and a car tyre, naming any one suitable mark a buyer should look for and what it tells the buyer.
questions.a: Any suitable tip, e.g. pulses: look for AGMARK, the certification mark for agricultural products (FSSAI shows food tested and safe); refrigerator: look for the BEE Star rating, since more stars mean less electricity (an ISI mark is also found on electrical appliances); car tyre: look for the ISI mark issued by BIS, which ensures quality and safe use. Each line must name a correct mark and what it tells the buyer.
s: Pulses with AGMARK or FSSAI and what it tells
Refrigerator with BEE Star rating or ISI and what it tells
Car tyre with the ISI mark and what it tells

questions.q:
The Menon family wants a new air conditioner and has two choices. A 3-star model costs Rs 38,000 and uses 1,500 units of electricity a year. A 5-star model costs Rs 46,000 and uses 1,000 units a year. A unit costs Rs 8. The family expects to live in the house for 5 years, but it has only Rs 40,000 in savings.
(a) Which label on the air conditioner tells the family which model uses less electricity, and which model does it favour?
(b) What is the yearly electricity bill for each model, and in how many years does the 5-star model recover its extra price?
(c) Besides the family's bill, what benefit does the chapter say lower electricity use brings?
(d) Which model should the family buy? Decide, using the total cost over 5 years, the savings limit and the chapter's point.
questions.a: (a) The BEE Star rating; it favours the 5-star model, since more stars mean less electricity. (b) 1,500 x 8 = Rs 12,000 and 1,000 x 8 = Rs 8,000; the extra price Rs 8,000 is recovered in 8,000 / 4,000 = 2 years. (c) It is good for the environment. (d) Over 5 years: 3-star 38,000 + 5 x 12,000 = Rs 98,000; 5-star 46,000 + 5 x 8,000 = Rs 86,000, so the 5-star model is cheaper by Rs 12,000 and uses less energy. Buy it if the family can arrange the extra Rs 6,000 beyond its savings; if it cannot, only the 3-star model is within its savings.
s: Part (a): BEE Star rating; 5-star model
Part (b): Rs 12,000 and Rs 8,000; 2 years
Part (c): good for the environment
Part (d): decision using Rs 98,000 against Rs 86,000, the savings limit and the chapter's point

questions.q: A website lists two electric kettles. Kettle A shows an ISI mark and has no reviews yet. Kettle B shows no mark and has 4.8 stars from 12 reviews. (a) From whom does each kettle's quality evidence come? (b) Which would you buy for a family with young children, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kettle A: the ISI mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards, a government agency. Kettle B: other consumers, through online reviews and feedback. (b) A reasoned choice: Kettle A, since the mark ensures quality and that the product is safe to use, whereas 12 reviews are few and are only opinions. Kettle B can be chosen only with the reasons that its reviews are more and consistent; the answer must use both kinds of evidence.
s: Part (a): ISI from a government agency, reviews from consumers
Part (b): a reasoned choice using both kinds of evidence

questions.q: Kabir says, 'A BEE Star rating on a laptop shows that the government has tested it and found it safe, in the same way as the FSSAI logo does for food.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Not at all. The chapter says the FSSAI logo indicates that food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume. BEE stands for Bureau of Energy Efficiency and its stars show how much electricity the product uses; higher stars mean less energy. The star rating is about energy efficiency, not a safety test.
s: Verdict: disagrees
States what FSSAI shows: food tested and safe
States that BEE stars show energy efficiency, not safety

questions.q: Compare certification marks with online reviews and word of mouth as ways of judging quality. Analyse the strengths of each and say which a consumer should depend on when buying medicine or food for the family.
questions.a: Certification marks like FSSAI, ISI and AGMARK are given by government agencies and confirm that a product meets minimum quality standards, so they are dependable for safety. Online reviews and word of mouth come from other buyers and build a product's reputation, helping a buyer decide whether to buy, but they are opinions and are not tested by an agency. For food and medicine, where health is involved, the family should rely first on the certification marks and then use reviews and word of mouth as support. The point that reviews are only opinions is reasoning, not a statement in the chapter.
s: Certification marks given by government agencies
They confirm minimum quality standards
Reviews and word of mouth shape reputation
Difference in reliability
A reasoned choice for food or medicine

questions.q: A packet of gram flour shows 12 June 2025 as the date of manufacture and a best before date six months later. (a) Work out the best before date. (b) A shopper with a food allergy sees the packet on 20 December 2025. Is it still within its best before date, and which other item on the label would she read first?
questions.a: (a) 12 December 2025. (b) No, 20 December 2025 is after 12 December 2025, so it is past the best before date. The allergen declaration is the item she would read first to see whether the food is safe for her.
s: Part (a): 12 December 2025
Part (b): past the date, and the allergen declaration read
